instructions: Scrub the taro under running water. Put it in a large pot, cover it with water, and bring it to a boil over high heat. Turn the heat to medium and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until a fork slides in easily but the taro isn't mushy. Smaller ones may take 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, put the rice in a fine strainer and rinse it under cold water. Transfer it to a medium saucepan with 2 1/4 cups water and a pinch of salt. Bring it to a boil, cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave the lid on for 5 minutes, then fluff it with a fork.
Finely chop the ginger and the green chili.
Drain the taro and rinse it under cold water until you can handle it. Peel off the skins and cut each one lengthwise into 1/4 to 1/2 inch slices. Pat the slices dry.

Heat 1 1/2 tbsp of the oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the taro slices in a single layer, working in two batches if they don't fit. Cook for about 10 minutes, turning once, until golden brown. Transfer them to a plate.
Heat the last 1 tbsp oil in the same skillet over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, then the ajwain. After about 20 seconds they will sizzle and smell toasty.
Add the ginger, green chili and curry leaves. Stir for 1 to 2 minutes, until the ginger starts to change color.
Return the taro to the pan. Add the turmeric, chili powder, coriander, amchur and salt. Sprinkle in 1 tbsp water and toss until the spices coat the taro.
Cook over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes. Chop 2 tbsp of the cilantro and stir it in.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
method_notes: No version of this dish had 20 or more ratings, so the lead is Cook With Manali's Simple Arbi Fry, which she says is also her arbi masala (5 from 7 ratings). It boils the taro, pan-fries the slices, then tempers cumin, ajwain, ginger, chili and curry leaves before adding the spices. Maayeka (3.67 from 6) and Nisha Madhulika (2.6 from 16) agree on boiling, peeling and crisping the taro with ajwain, but cook it in a pressure cooker. This version doubles the lead's ajwain to 1/2 tsp, since the other sources use 1 tsp or more. Hebbar's Kitchen has a dum arbi gravy, a different dish, and is not used.
